item.text:
**The all-male panel is worth raising, but it is not, by itself, proof of discrimination.** It is a reason to ask how the broadcaster ensured a fair selection process—and whether the panel’s composition complied with its recruitment and equality policies.

Your longer experience and five years as deputy news editor give you a reasonable basis to seek a substantive explanation. But years served alone don’t establish who best met the role’s criteria. Digital expertise could legitimately carry significant weight; the important questions are whether that was an advertised criterion and whether it was assessed consistently, rather than introduced to justify the decision afterward.

I would follow up now, calmly and in writing, asking for:
- The selection criteria and their weighting.
- Your assessment against those criteria, and the reasons the successful candidate was preferred, subject to privacy limits.
- The policy on selection-panel composition and how fairness was safeguarded.
- The review or complaint procedure and any deadlines.

You could frame the panel issue like this:

> “I also note that the selection panel consisted entirely of men. Could you confirm whether this complied with the broadcaster’s recruitment and equality policies, and what measures were used to ensure an impartial assessment?”

Two weeks without a reply warrants a reminder, but silence alone doesn’t establish wrongdoing. Keep the advert, application, correspondence and notes of your interviews. If you may want to challenge the outcome, speak to your union or a local employment adviser promptly: **complaint deadlines may run while you’re waiting for an explanation.**

Which country is this in? Rules on public-sector appointments, panel composition and entitlement to reasons vary considerably.
